stem: Production data shows that in 12% of cases, your agent skips get_customer entirely and calls lookup_order using only the customer's stated name, occasionally leading to misidentified accounts and incorrect refunds. What change would most effectively address this reliability issue?

options.text: Add a programmatic prerequisite that blocks lookup_order and process_refund calls until get_customer has returned a verified customer ID.
options.why: When a specific tool sequence is required for critical business logic, programmatic enforcement provides the deterministic guarantee that prompt-based approaches cannot; the skip rate becomes zero rather than merely smaller.

options.text: Enhance the system prompt to state that customer verification via get_customer is mandatory before any order operations.
options.why: A stronger instruction relies on probabilistic LLM compliance, which is insufficient when the errors have financial consequences.

options.text: Add few-shot examples showing the agent always calling get_customer first, even when customers volunteer order details.
options.why: Examples also work through probabilistic compliance; they may lower the 12% but cannot eliminate misidentified refunds.

options.text: Implement a routing classifier that analyzes each request and enables only the subset of tools appropriate for that request type.
options.why: A routing classifier addresses tool availability rather than tool ordering; the problem is that verification is skipped, not that the wrong tools are exposed.

explanation: When a specific tool sequence is required for critical business logic (like verifying customer identity before processing refunds), programmatic enforcement provides deterministic guarantees that prompt-based approaches cannot. Prompt and few-shot approaches rely on probabilistic LLM compliance, which is insufficient when errors have financial consequences, and a routing classifier solves tool availability rather than ordering.
reference: CCAR-F Exam Guide — Task 1.4; Claude Agent SDK docs — Hooks

stem: Production logs show the agent frequently calls get_customer when users ask about orders (e.g., "check my order #12345"), instead of calling lookup_order. Both tools have minimal descriptions ("Retrieves customer information" / "Retrieves order details") and accept similar identifier formats. What's the most effective first step to improve tool selection reliability?

options.text: Add few-shot examples to the system prompt demonstrating correct tool selection patterns, with 5-8 examples showing order-related queries routing to lookup_order.
options.why: Few-shot examples add token overhead on every request without fixing the underlying issue, which is that the tool descriptions do not differentiate the tools.

options.text: Expand each tool's description to include input formats it handles, example queries, edge cases, and boundaries explaining when to use it versus similar tools.
options.why: Tool descriptions are the primary mechanism LLMs use for tool selection; richer descriptions address the root cause with a low-effort, high-leverage change.

options.text: Implement a routing layer that parses user input before each turn and pre-selects the appropriate tool based on detected keywords and identifier patterns.
options.why: A routing layer is over-engineered and bypasses the LLM's natural language understanding, which is exactly what should be doing the selection.

options.text: Consolidate both tools into a single lookup_entity tool that accepts any identifier and internally determines which backend to query.
options.why: Consolidation is a valid architectural choice but requires far more effort than a first step warrants when the immediate problem is inadequate descriptions.

explanation: Tool descriptions are the primary mechanism LLMs use for tool selection. When descriptions are minimal, models lack the context to differentiate between similar tools, so expanding the descriptions with input formats, example queries, edge cases and boundaries is the low-effort, high-leverage first fix.
reference: Claude API docs — Define tools; Anthropic — Writing tools for agents

stem: Your agent achieves 55% first-contact resolution, well below the 80% target. Logs show it escalates straightforward cases (standard damage replacements with photo evidence) while attempting to autonomously handle complex situations requiring policy exceptions. What's the most effective way to improve escalation calibration?

options.text: Add explicit escalation criteria to your system prompt with few-shot examples demonstrating when to escalate versus resolve autonomously.
options.why: The root cause is unclear decision boundaries; explicit criteria plus examples fix that directly and are the proportionate first response before adding infrastructure.

options.text: Have the agent self-report a confidence score (1-10) before each response and automatically route requests to humans when confidence falls below a threshold.
options.why: LLM self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated, and the agent is already incorrectly confident on the hard cases, so a confidence threshold would not catch them.

options.text: Deploy a separate classifier model trained on historical tickets to predict which requests need escalation before the main agent begins processing.
options.why: A trained classifier is over-engineered, requiring labeled data and ML infrastructure, when prompt optimization has not yet been tried.

options.text: Implement sentiment analysis to detect customer frustration levels and automatically escalate when negative sentiment exceeds a threshold.
options.why: Sentiment solves a different problem entirely; it does not correlate with case complexity, which is the actual issue.

explanation: Adding explicit escalation criteria with few-shot examples directly addresses the root cause: unclear decision boundaries. Self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated, a separate classifier is over-engineered before prompt optimization has been tried, and sentiment does not track case complexity.
reference: CCAR-F Exam Guide — Task 5.2; Claude API docs — Prompt engineering overview

stem: You want to create a custom /review slash command that runs your team's standard code review checklist. This command should be available to every developer when they clone or pull the repository. Where should you create this command file?

options.text: In the .claude/commands/ directory in the project repository
options.why: Project-scoped commands live in `.claude/commands/` inside the repository, so they are version-controlled and automatically available to everyone who clones or pulls.

options.text: In ~/.claude/commands/ in each developer's home directory
options.why: The home-directory location holds personal commands that are not shared through version control, so each developer would have to install it separately.

options.text: In the CLAUDE.md file at the project root
options.why: CLAUDE.md carries project instructions and context, not slash command definitions.

options.text: In a .claude/config.json file with a commands array
options.why: This describes a configuration mechanism that does not exist in Claude Code.

explanation: Project-scoped custom slash commands are stored in the `.claude/commands/` directory within the repository, where they are version-controlled and automatically available to all developers. `~/.claude/commands/` is for personal commands, CLAUDE.md holds instructions rather than commands, and there is no commands array in a config file.

stem: You've been assigned to restructure the team's monolithic application into microservices. This will involve changes across dozens of files and requires decisions about service boundaries and module dependencies. Which approach should you take?

options.text: Enter plan mode to explore the codebase, understand dependencies, and design an implementation approach before making changes.
options.why: Plan mode is designed for large-scale changes with multiple valid approaches and architectural decisions; it allows safe exploration and design before committing to changes.

options.text: Start with direct execution and make changes incrementally, letting the implementation reveal the natural service boundaries.
options.why: Discovering dependencies late through implementation risks costly rework across dozens of files.

options.text: Use direct execution with comprehensive upfront instructions detailing exactly how each service should be structured.
options.why: This assumes you already know the right structure without having explored the code, which is precisely what still needs to be determined.

options.text: Begin in direct execution mode and only switch to plan mode if you encounter unexpected complexity during implementation.
options.why: The complexity is already stated in the requirements; it is not something that might emerge later.

explanation: Plan mode is designed for complex tasks involving large-scale changes, multiple valid approaches and architectural decisions, exactly what a monolith-to-microservices restructuring requires. It enables safe codebase exploration and design before committing to changes.
reference: Claude Code docs — Common workflows (plan mode)

stem: Your codebase has distinct areas with different coding conventions: React components use functional style with hooks, API handlers use async/await with specific error handling, and database models follow a repository pattern. Test files are spread throughout the codebase alongside the code they test (e.g., Button.test.tsx next to Button.tsx), and you want all tests to follow the same conventions regardless of location. What's the most maintainable way to ensure Claude automatically applies the correct conventions when generating code?

options.text: Create rule files in .claude/rules/ with YAML frontmatter specifying glob patterns to conditionally apply conventions based on file paths
options.why: Rules with glob patterns such as `**/*.test.tsx` apply conventions automatically by file path regardless of directory, which is essential for test files spread throughout the codebase.

options.text: Consolidate all conventions in the root CLAUDE.md file under headers for each area, relying on Claude to infer which section applies
options.why: This relies on inference rather than explicit matching, making it unreliable and loading every convention into every session.

options.text: Create skills in .claude/skills/ for each code type that include the relevant conventions in their SKILL.md files
options.why: Skills require manual invocation or rely on Claude choosing to load them, which contradicts the need for deterministic automatic application based on file paths.

options.text: Place a separate CLAUDE.md file in each subdirectory containing that area's specific conventions
options.why: CLAUDE.md files are directory-bound, so they cannot easily handle test files spread across many directories.

explanation: `.claude/rules/` files with glob patterns in their frontmatter apply conventions automatically based on file paths regardless of directory location, which is what co-located test files need. Root-level headers rely on inference, skills are not path-triggered, and per-directory CLAUDE.md files are directory-bound.
reference: Claude Code docs — Memory (rules and path-specific instructions)

stem: After running the system on the topic "impact of AI on creative industries," you observe that each subagent completes successfully: the web search agent finds relevant articles, the document analysis agent summarizes papers correctly, and the synthesis agent produces coherent output. However, the final reports cover only visual arts, completely missing music, writing, and film production. When you examine the coordinator's logs, you see it decomposed the topic into three subtasks: "AI in digital art creation," "AI in graphic design," and "AI in photography." What is the most likely root cause?

options.text: The synthesis agent lacks instructions for identifying coverage gaps in the findings it receives from other agents.
options.why: The synthesis agent worked correctly on what it was given; it cannot create findings for domains that were never researched.

options.text: The coordinator agent's task decomposition is too narrow, resulting in subagent assignments that don't cover all relevant domains of the topic.
options.why: The coordinator's logs show the root cause directly: it decomposed "creative industries" into only visual-arts subtasks, omitting music, writing and film.

options.text: The web search agent's queries are not comprehensive enough and need to be expanded to cover more creative industry sectors.
options.why: The web search agent executed its assigned subtasks correctly; the problem is what it was assigned, not how it searched.

options.text: The document analysis agent is filtering out sources related to non-visual creative industries due to overly restrictive relevance criteria.
options.why: There were no non-visual sources to filter because the coordinator never assigned those areas; the analysis agent worked within its scope.

explanation: The coordinator's logs reveal the root cause directly: it decomposed "creative industries" into only visual-arts subtasks (digital art, graphic design, photography), omitting music, writing and film. The subagents executed their assigned tasks correctly; the problem is what they were assigned.
reference: CCAR-F Exam Guide — Task 1.2; Anthropic — How we built our multi-agent research system

stem: The web search subagent times out while researching a complex topic. You need to design how this failure information flows back to the coordinator agent. Which error propagation approach best enables intelligent recovery?

options.text: Return structured error context to the coordinator including the failure type, the attempted query, any partial results, and potential alternative approaches.
options.why: Structured error context gives the coordinator what it needs to decide whether to retry with a modified query, try an alternative approach or proceed with partial results.

options.text: Implement automatic retry logic with exponential backoff within the subagent, returning a generic "search unavailable" status only after all retries are exhausted.
options.why: A generic status hides valuable context from the coordinator and prevents informed recovery decisions.

options.text: Catch the timeout within the subagent and return an empty result set marked as successful.
options.why: Marking failure as success suppresses the error, prevents any recovery and risks incomplete research outputs.

options.text: Propagate the timeout exception directly to a top-level handler that terminates the entire research workflow.
options.why: Terminating the whole workflow is unnecessary when recovery strategies such as a modified query or partial results could succeed.

explanation: Structured error context gives the coordinator the information it needs to make intelligent recovery decisions. Generic statuses hide context, marking failures as success prevents recovery, and terminating the entire workflow discards recoverable work.

stem: During testing, you observe that the synthesis agent frequently needs to verify specific claims while combining findings. Currently, when verification is needed, the synthesis agent returns control to the coordinator, which invokes the web search agent, then re-invokes synthesis with results. This adds 2-3 round trips per task and increases latency by 40%. Your evaluation shows that 85% of these verifications are simple fact-checks (dates, names, statistics) while 15% require deeper investigation. What's the most effective approach to reduce overhead while maintaining system reliability?

options.text: Give the synthesis agent a scoped verify_fact tool for simple lookups, while complex verifications continue delegating to the web search agent through the coordinator.
options.why: This applies least privilege: the synthesis agent gets only what it needs for the 85% common case while the coordination pattern is preserved for complex cases.

options.text: Have the synthesis agent accumulate all verification needs and return them as a batch to the coordinator at the end of its pass, which then sends them all to the web search agent at once.
options.why: Batching creates blocking dependencies because later synthesis steps may depend on facts verified earlier in the pass.

options.text: Give the synthesis agent access to all web search tools so it can handle any verification need directly without round-trips through the coordinator.
options.why: Granting all search tools over-provisions the synthesis agent and violates separation of concerns.

options.text: Have the web search agent proactively cache extra context around each source during initial research, anticipating what the synthesis agent might need to verify.
options.why: Speculative caching cannot reliably predict what the synthesis agent will need to verify.

explanation: A scoped `verify_fact` tool applies the principle of least privilege: the synthesis agent gets only what it needs for the common simple case while complex verifications still flow through the coordinator. Batching creates blocking dependencies, granting all search tools over-provisions the agent, and speculative caching cannot predict verification needs.

stem: Your pipeline script runs `claude "Analyze this pull request for security issues"` but the job hangs indefinitely. Logs indicate Claude Code is waiting for interactive input. What's the correct approach to run Claude Code in an automated pipeline?

options.text: Add the -p flag: claude -p "Analyze this pull request for security issues"
options.why: `-p` (or `--print`) is the documented non-interactive mode: it processes the prompt, writes the result to stdout and exits without waiting for input.

options.text: Set the environment variable CLAUDE_HEADLESS=true before running the command
options.why: There is no `CLAUDE_HEADLESS` environment variable; this references a feature that does not exist.

options.text: Redirect stdin from /dev/null: claude "Analyze this pull request for security issues" < /dev/null
options.why: A Unix stdin workaround does not address Claude Code's command syntax; the interactive session still starts.

options.text: Add the --batch flag: claude --batch "Analyze this pull request for security issues"
options.why: There is no `--batch` flag in Claude Code.

explanation: The `-p` (or `--print`) flag is the documented way to run Claude Code in non-interactive mode: it processes the prompt, outputs the result to stdout and exits without waiting for user input, which is what CI/CD pipelines require. The other options reference non-existent features or use workarounds that do not change the command's mode.
reference: Claude Code docs — CLI reference; Run Claude Code programmatically (headless)

stem: Your team wants to reduce API costs for automated analysis. Currently, real-time Claude calls power two workflows: (1) a blocking pre-merge check that must complete before developers can merge, and (2) a technical debt report generated overnight for review the next morning. Your manager proposes switching both to the Message Batches API for its 50% cost savings. How should you evaluate this proposal?

options.text: Use batch processing for the technical debt reports only; keep real-time calls for pre-merge checks.
options.why: Batches have no guaranteed latency and can take up to 24 hours, which suits an overnight report but not a check developers are waiting on.

options.text: Switch both workflows to batch processing with status polling to check for completion.
options.why: Relying on batches usually finishing faster is not acceptable for a blocking workflow with no latency guarantee.

options.text: Keep real-time calls for both workflows to avoid batch result ordering issues.
options.why: This reflects a misconception: batch results can be correlated using `custom_id` fields, so ordering is not a reason to forgo the savings.

options.text: Switch both to batch processing with a timeout fallback to real-time if batches take too long.
options.why: A fallback adds unnecessary complexity when the simpler solution is matching each API to its appropriate use case.

explanation: The Message Batches API offers 50% cost savings but has processing times up to 24 hours with no guaranteed latency SLA. That makes it unsuitable for blocking pre-merge checks where developers wait, but ideal for overnight jobs like technical debt reports. Batch results are matched with `custom_id`, so ordering is not a concern.

stem: A pull request modifies 14 files across the stock tracking module. Your single-pass review analyzing all files together produces inconsistent results: detailed feedback for some files but superficial comments for others, obvious bugs missed, and contradictory feedback—flagging a pattern as problematic in one file while approving identical code elsewhere in the same PR. How should you restructure the review?

options.text: Split into focused passes: analyze each file individually for local issues, then run a separate integration-focused pass examining cross-file data flow.
options.why: Focused passes address the root cause, attention dilution across many files: file-by-file analysis gives consistent depth and a separate integration pass catches cross-file issues.

options.text: Require developers to split large PRs into smaller submissions of 3-4 files before the automated review runs.
options.why: This shifts the burden to developers without improving the review system itself.

options.text: Switch to a higher-tier model with a larger context window to give all 14 files adequate attention in one pass.
options.why: A larger context window does not solve attention quality; the files already fit, the problem is dilution.

options.text: Run three independent review passes on the full PR and only flag issues that appear in at least two of the three runs.
options.why: Requiring consensus would suppress detection of real bugs that are only caught intermittently, making the review worse.

explanation: Splitting reviews into focused passes directly addresses attention dilution when processing many files at once. File-by-file analysis ensures consistent depth, and a separate integration pass catches cross-file issues. Pushing the problem onto developers, larger context windows and consensus voting do not fix attention quality.
reference: CCAR-F Exam Guide — Task 4.6; Anthropic — Building effective agents (prompt chaining)
